 Can Maryland football get off to a winning restart vs. Illinois?
 Maryland football makes his post-Mike Locksley debut Saturday at noon against Illinois at SECU Stadium (FS1). The Terps are 2-5 overall and 0-4 in the Big Ten, and this opens a five-game stretch against Illinois.
 Jeff Ermann 4 Maryland football makes his post-Mike Locksley debut Saturday at noon against Illinois at SECU Stadium (FS1). The Terps are 2-5 overall and 0-4 in the Big Ten, and this opens a five-game stretch against an Illini team that has won two straight after a 2-3 start.
 Jeremy Werner, publisher of IlliniInquirer.com, answered questions below on freshman quarterback Michael Clayton II, receiver Collin Dixon , a defense that changed coordinators in the middle of the season and where the game could turn. Werner expects a grind and picks Illinois, 26-24.
 Bret Bielema signed a seven-year extension before the 2025 season and has the Illini winning at a level the program hadn't sustained in decades. Six years in, what is the fan sentiment on the job he's doing? 
 Bret Bielema is the most successful coach at Illinois in two generations, so his approval rating is incredibly high and it should be. He hasn't been perfect and made a terrible defensive coordinator hire this past offseason, but Bielema largely has awoken a program that most have long considered a "sleeping giant."
 While the Illini haven't become a powerhouse like Curt Cignetti at Indiana , he is bringing sustained success to Illinois, making three bowl games in four years, including a record 19 wins over the previous two seasons, which included the program's first wins over SEC opponents in bowl games ( South Carolina and Tennessee ). If he leads Illinois to a bowl game this season, it'll be the first time since 1992 that Illinois has made three straight bowl games.
 Now, Bielema has come one win short of bowls in two seasons (2021 and 2023) and still must get two more wins this season. But this program is no longer a bottom-tier program, which it had been for most of the 21st century before he arrived.
 The Illini still have to do more with less compared to the Big Ten powers, but Bielema has started to build a program that looks like what Minnesota has been under P.J. Fleck and has shades of what Kirk Ferentz has done at Iowa. That was the idea when they hired him.
 Before he arrived, Illinois routinely had half-filled stadiums. Now, Illinois is selling out games more often than not. Basketball is still king at Illinois, but falls have been a lot more fun and interesting in Champaign under Bielema.
 Since the Hauck split, the Illini lost to Purdue at home, survived Michigan State 38-37 in overtime and then held Oregon to 10 points. What's changed schematically or in personnel to explain that turnaround, and how much of the Oregon performance is real versus an Oregon offense that had been sputtering? 
 Something had to be rotten for Bielema to part ways with his first-year coordinator just four games into a two-year contract, and the more we hear from players and coaches, the more that becomes clear. Illinois had a ton of communication issues under Hauck, a longtime FCS head coach who had never been a play-caller, and the Illini's players almost all took a step back in production. They weren't playing confident or fast.
 Cooper hasn't suddenly turned a group with suspect talent into world beaters, but they are far more competent. Mental errors, missed assignments and missed tackles are down. The Illini are clearly playing faster, and they're starting to be more disruptive. They're getting a bit more pressure and punching the ball out a bit the last few games, albeit against two bad offenses in Michigan State and Oregon, and they've made some slight personnel changes that have helped. They rotate fewer linebackers, allowing James Kreutz and Ismael Kante to stay on the field for most of the game. They also moved cornerback Tanner Heckel to safety to replace the struggling Mac Resetich , helping settle a secondary that had underachieved its talent during the first five games of the season.
 It's all relative, as MSU and Oregon are bad offenses, and Michigan State put up a lot of points in the second half against Illinois. The Illini still lack talent up front and can get out-athleted in space. But they are more competitive and have made enough plays the last two games to help a good offense win games.
 Katin Houser broke his hand against Michigan State, then freshman Michael Clayton II beat Oregon in his first career start. What does Clayton do well that Maryland should prepare for? 
 Michael Clayton II has had some freshman moments, as should be expected. But he has thrown four touchdown passes to just one turnover in five quarters (plus overtime at MSU), and that turnover was a fumble where he got hit hard by Oregon star Teium Tuioti.
 The Illini have shown confidence in Clayton to rip some throws into tight coverage in money situations, and he's been really good in the red zone and on third down so far. He has a really strong arm and can rip it with velocity. He's put a few into some dangerous windows, but he's gotten away with it so far. He has overthrown a few, but veteran wideouts Collin Dixon and Hudson Clement have helped him by winning some contested catches. Clayton is thinner, so ball security is a question mark when he gets sacked, something that is worth monitoring against Maryland's talented underclassmen edge rushers.
 The Illini also ran the ball incredibly well against Oregon to help ease some pressure on Clayton, and the offensive line is really finding its physicality after making a lineup change before MSU. Aidan Laughery is a really good running back with speed to take it to the house when he gets the edge. Meanwhile, Jordan Anderson and Javari Barnett give some physicality between the tackles. Also, Illinois has rotated sophomore quarterback Carson Boyd at times for Clayton. He's built like Demond Williams Jr. and is a big running threat, though Illinois will let him pass as a counter, so that's worth watching this game too.
 Clayton isn't as reliable as Houser, obviously. Some mistakes are expected, and the Illini likely will be more of a running team with a freshman quarterback than the downfield passing team it was with Houser. But Clayton has shown arm strength and poise so far.
 Also, Barry Lunney Jr. is one of the best offensive coordinators that few talk about in the country. I think he's a competitive advantage in most games and has put his players in great positions in most games.
 Collin Dixon came into the Oregon game with 608 receiving yards and nine touchdowns, then caught the game-sealing score. Should he be Maryland's top concern on defense and who else should they focus on? 
 Collin Dixon is the best offensive player on the field on Saturday. He isn't the biggest, but he isn't small (6-foot-1, 215 pounds). He isn't the fastest, but he isn't slow. Yet, Dixon is a complete wide receiver who gets the most out of his talent. He's known as one of the hardest workers on the team and is an absolute tactician as a route runner. He's physical as a blocker, and he probably has the best hands I've seen in my 15 years covering Illinois, and that includes Pat Bryant , who was a third-round pick a few years ago. Simply, when the Illini get a one-on-one opportunity, they're going to Dixon, and it almost always results in a win.
 He also creates a lot of attention, which opens up opportunities for the Illini run game and No. 2 wideout Hudson Clement, who has a lot of similarities to Dixon in that he doesn't have an elite trait but is just a very productive veteran. Illinois is just as comfortable going to him as Dixon. Slot receiver Brayden Trimble has been solid as a sophomore but doesn't get targeted a lot. The tight ends are mostly check-down targets, though former starting running back Kaden Feagin remains an intriguing athlete at tight end.
 The other top weapon is Aidan Laughery, a fifth-year who has finally stayed healthy this season and is leading the Big Ten in yards per carry among backs with at least 50 carries. He had 100-plus yards against both Ohio State and Oregon, so he has a chance to be an All-Big Ten back if he keeps this up. Freshman Javari Barnett might be their most talented back due to his mix of size and burst, but he just isn't as reliable or experienced, so he doesn't get a lot of reps.
 Illinois has only two interceptions this season and has struggled defending fourth downs. Where do you see this game being won or lost and what would you say is Illinois' biggest strength and weakness? 
 When Illinois gets a takeaway, it is 4-0 this season. When it doesn't, it's 0-3. They also have 4.0 sacks and four forced fumbles during the last two games after totaling just 2.0 sacks and zero forced fumbles against the previous four FBS opponents. They've gotten slightly better lately on third down too.
 Simply, Illinois needs to continue to create more timely negative plays just to limit an opponent's possessions and red-zone opportunities. Down-to-down, this isn't a very good defense due to a lack of talent up front. They can get overpowered on the defensive line and the linebackers aren't the best athletes.
 The secondary has underachieved but seems to be settling in with Heckel, one of the team's athletes, recently moving to free safety. Matthew Bailey is an All-Big Ten safety and a hybrid linebacker/safety type who is used as a pass rusher, a thumper in the run game and as someone who can cover tight ends. He is the Illini's best player, and former All-Big Ten defensive backs Juice Clarke and Xavier Scott have played better the last few weeks following Hauck's exit.
 But the idea of this 3-3-5 defense was to create more disruption. They've shown more flashes of that in the last three games under Cooper. That'll have to continue to win a third straight game.
 The Illini have Nebraska , UCLA , Iowa and Northwestern left after this. What's a realistic finish from here, and what's your score prediction for Saturday? 
 After a wholly disappointing 2-3 start that included allowing Purdue to end a 19-game Big Ten losing streak, getting to a bowl game would be a great outcome for Illinois. Most thought Illinois would take a step back after losing a special senior class that led Illinois to its winningest two-year stretch in program history. But this season looked headed for a potential bottoming out as Michigan State forced overtime after Illinois had built a 23-7 lead late in the third quarter. Credit to Bielema, his staff and his players for bouncing back and finding ways to get two wins to give this season renewed life.
 But this game against Maryland looks necessary to get to a bowl. This is by far the most winnable game against a team that has replaced its head coach and defensive coordinator. While I expect Maryland to feel refreshed after an off week with pressure lifted with its coach already fired, Illinois has played better and more competitive ball this season. The Illini can't follow up a statement win over Oregon with a road loss at Maryland, especially with Illinois likely an underdog in its final four games against Nebraska, at No. 7 UCLA, vs. Iowa and at No. 20 Northwestern.
 Beat Maryland and Illinois needs to just find one more win to get a bowl game, and I think that's possible, especially in its home games against Nebraska and Iowa. Lose, and it's hard to see Illinois getting that third straight bowl game, though nothing in CFB seems predictable right now.
 I expect this game to be more of a grind than some may think.
 As weird as it is to say, Maryland's offense is better than Oregon's and I still have lingering doubts about this defense's quality. I do expect Illinois to be able to run against Maryland, but Illinois is still starting a freshman quarterback, and that's always a roll of the dice.
 I'm picking Illinois to win because I think there's a big coaching advantage, but I think it'll be a nail-biter. Illinois 26, Maryland 24.
